preamble: Debuccalization of the voiceless velar fricative [x] to the glottal fricative [h]: the tongue-body constriction is lost and only glottal friction remains. Proto-Germanic */x/ (from PIE *k by Grimm's law) became [h] word-initially in the daughter languages; Spanish /x/ (spelled j, g) is [h] in Andalusia, the Canary Islands, the Caribbean and much of lowland Spanish America; Old Anatolian Turkish ḫ [x] merged with /h/ in Turkish; and Swahili replaces Arabic ḵ [x] with h in loanwords.

examples.note: Germanic word-initial /x/ and /xʷ/ were reduced to /h/ and /hʷ/; Gothic and Old Norse show the same initial h.
Word-initial reflex; medial and final /x/ stayed velar in Old English (as in niht 'night').
/x/ is pronounced [h] in western Andalusia, Extremadura, the Canaries, the Caribbean, Central America, Venezuela and coastal Colombia and Ecuador; eastern Andalusia keeps [x].
The same realization before front vowels, where /x/ is spelled ⟨g⟩.

examples.from: Old Anatolian Turkish ḫaber [x] 'news' (< Arabic ḵabar)
examples.note: The velar fricative of Old Anatolian Turkish merged with /h/ in modern Standard Turkish.
Inherited through Ottoman Turkish with initial [h].
Loanword adaptation; the standard orthography deliberately dropped the earlier ⟨kh⟩ spelling, though some speakers keep [x].
Same substitution of [h] for the Arabic velar fricative.
